titre_video: The US Dollar Collapse in Real Time (Day by Day)

segments.titre: Hook: the dollar is dead and savings are about to vanish
segments.resume: The video opens with the claim that the dollar is dead, global markets are panicking and millions of Americans face irreversible financial chaos. It frames what follows as a day-by-day account of a collapse that has already started.
segments.texte: The dollar is dead. Global markets are panicking and your life savings are about to vanish. There are no warnings, no explanations, just millions of Americans plunged into total, irreversible financial chaos. And the worst part? It’s already started… and no one has told you what comes next.

segments.titre: Day 1: Maggie Castellano and the $42 billion bond sale
segments.resume: At 12.52pm on a Tuesday, Maggie Castellano of the Treasury's Office of Debt Management is eating a turkey sandwich. At one o'clock the country must sell $42 billion in 10-year bonds, described as America's IOUs.
segments.texte: Day 1 It’s 12.52pm on a Tuesday afternoon. Tucked away in the corner of the Treasury Department, Maggie Castellano is holding a half eaten turkey sandwich over her keyboard. Maggie works in the Office of Debt Management, She’s one of the people responsible for borrowing the money that keeps the U.S. economy alive. At exactly one o'clock, the country needs to sell $42 billion in 10-year bonds. Think of them like America’s IOUs.

segments.titre: Dollar dominance and Maggie's 68% foreign buyer forecast
segments.resume: The dollar sits on one side of 89% of all currency trades, and countries park huge reserves in American IOUs that pay interest. Maggie has spent 25 years predicting who buys the debt and expects foreign buyers to take 68% today.
segments.texte: The dollar is king. And the world knows it. It sits is on one side of 89% of all the currency trades on Earth. Countries end up sitting on enormous piles of money, and the safest place to park it is an American IOU that pays you interest while you wait. Maggie has spent 25 years predicting who shows up to buy this debt. Today she has foreign buyers down for 68%.

segments.titre: The failed auction: foreign buyers take 41%, dealers 34%
segments.resume: The results show foreign buyers took only 41% instead of 68%, and the remaining billions were forced onto primary dealers, who took 34% instead of the expected 12%. America had to raise its interest rates to sweeten the deal, the worst auction failure of Maggie's career.
segments.texte: At 1.01 p.m., the results hit her screen. Maggie can read a multi-billion dollar auction in 4 seconds. This time she stares for 30. The foreign buyers didn’t show up. They didn’t take 68%. They took 41. The remaining billions were forced onto a handful of major US banks, the primary dealers legally required to hoover up whatever toxic debt nobody wants. Maggie expected them to take 12%. They took 34%. To force people to take on the debt, America had to jack up its interest rates. It needed to sweeten the deal. It’s the worst auction failure she’s seen in her career. The U.S. essentially had a fire sale, and the biggest customers walked away.

segments.titre: Warning signs and the March 2020 precedent
segments.resume: The 10-year rate was already above 5.3%, near a 2-decade high, the Treasury doubled its long-term debt buybacks and oil was over $100 a barrel. In March 2020 foreign holders dumped almost $300 billion of Treasuries in a month, but the Fed stepped in and the buyers came back because they had nowhere else to go.
segments.texte: The market has been spluttering for months. The 10-year rate was already above 5.3%, close to its highest in 2 decades. The Treasury doubled how much of its own long-term debt it was buying back to make the markets look busy. Oil is over $100 a barrel which has added another glaze of gloominess over the global economy. Still, Maggie has seen ugly days. In March 2020, foreign holders dumped almost $300 billion of Treasuries in a single month. The Fed stepped in, and within a few weeks the buyers were back, because the buyers always come back. They have nowhere else to go.

segments.titre: Maggie's press line and Tom's bike shop shipment
segments.resume: Twenty minutes after the auction, Maggie types a press line saying the auction was well-received and the market orderly. At home her husband Tom, who owns a bike shop, complains about a fuel surcharge on a container of carbon frames from China, while she pretends the financial world is not cracking.
segments.texte: 20 minutes later, the Secretary's office demands a line for the press briefing. Maggie types the lie without looking at the keys: “The auction was well-received, and the Treasury market remains deep, liquid, and orderly.” Maggie goes home, has dinner while her husband, Tom, complains. He owns a bike shop and a container of carbon frames from China is somewhere east of Hawaii. The shipping company has just tacked on a fuel surcharge, which Tom describes as piracy. Maggie just smiles and pretends the financial world isn’t cracking.

segments.titre: Tokyo opens: the yen falls and Japan starts selling
segments.resume: By 9.45 p.m. Tokyo's markets open and the first domino falls. The yen is near a 40-year low, Japan spent $59 billion in July buying its own currency, and Maggie's biggest customer has started selling Treasuries rather than just stopping its purchases.
segments.texte: By 9.45 p.m., Tokyo’s markets are open. And the first domino falls. The yen is near a 40-year low, and in July Japan spent $59 billion buying its own currency to keep it from sinking further. Basically, Maggie's biggest customer didn’t just stop buying… they started selling.

segments.titre: Gulf oil company accepts yuan and gold; money flees America
segments.resume: Just after 2 in the morning a state owned Persian Gulf oil company says it will accept Chinese yuan and gold for crude. Money that normally floods into America in a scare is now fleeing, which threatens the premise that buyers always come back, and Maggie starts a short list of who will still lend to America.
segments.texte: Just after 2 in the morning, Maggie’s phone lights up. A state owned oil company in the Persian Gulf says it will accept Chinese yuan and gold for its crude. It takes 2 minutes to process what is going on and she jerks awake. Normally, when the world gets scared, money floods into America because it's the safest harbor. Tonight, the money is fleeing. Maggie stumbles downstairs and opens her laptop at the kitchen table and stares at a blank page. Her 25 year career rests on one single premise: the buyers always come back because they have nowhere else to go. At 2.30 in the morning, Maggie starts a list of who's still willing to give America money to keep the lights on. It's a short list.

segments.titre: Day 2: "Sell America" and exploding interest rates
segments.resume: On Wednesday the stock market is in freefall while the dollar and Treasuries crash at the same time, a scenario traders call Sell America. With no demand for America's IOUs, interest rates explode and credit cards, mortgages and loans skyrocket.
segments.texte: Day 2 Wednesday morning. The stock market is in freefall. But that’s not the terrifying part. The panic is happening elsewhere. The dollar, stock and America's IOUs are all crashing at the same time. Traders have a name for this nightmare scenario. “Sell America.” When no one wants America’s IOUs, interest rates explode. Credit cards, mortgages and loans skyrocket across the country.

segments.titre: Maggie's second official lie and Tom's cancelled mortgage
segments.resume: At noon Maggie types another statement that markets remain orderly. At the same moment Tom receives an email from his mortgage broker cancelling the loan quoted at 7.1% that was meant to fund opening a bike shop, due to market conditions.
segments.texte: At noon, Maggie is at the Treasury typing out another official lie for the evening news: “Markets remain orderly.” At that exact moment, Maggie’s husband Tom gets a 3 sentence email from his mortgage broker. Two weeks ago, he was quoted 7.1% to refinance the house and borrow enough to open a bike shop. Today, the loan has been canceled due to market conditions.

segments.titre: The bank kill list: Chesapeake Federal and the SVB precedent
segments.resume: In a windowless conference room an Office of the Comptroller of the Currency official shows 11 regional banks facing insolvency, since banks hold Treasuries whose older issues lost value after rates spiked. Chesapeake Federal, the Castellanos' bank for 19 years, is fourth; Maggie recalls that in 2023 Silicon Valley Bank lost $42 billion of deposits in one day and was gone within about 48 hours.
segments.texte: By 9.45 p.m., she's trapped in a windowless conference room. Someone from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, the agency that monitors the banking system, puts a list on the screen. It’s worth noting that banks don’t keep your money in a vault. They park it in America's IOUs. But because interest rates just spiked, the older IOUs are worth pennies on the dollar. The screen shows 11 regional banks that are facing immediate insolvency. Fourth on the kill list is Chesapeake Federal, where Maggie and her family have banked for 19 years. Maggie knows what happens next. In 2023, Silicon Valley Bank loaded up on IOUs, rates went up, and the IOUs lost value. When word got out, customers pulled $42 billion in a single day. The bank was gone about 48 hours after it admitted it had a problem.

segments.titre: Maggie tells Tom to move $380,000: insider trading
segments.resume: Maggie wakes Tom, whose business account at Chesapeake Federal holds $380,000, and tells him to move every cent by the end of the next day and tell no one. This is illegal, since federal employees may not use nonpublic information for private gain, so she has committed federal insider trading.
segments.texte: Maggie rushes home at 11.15 p.m, Tom's asleep on the couch with the news on mute. His business account at Chesapeake Federal holds $380,000, every dollar he needs to pay global suppliers. Maggie wakes him up, looks him in the eye and tells him to move every single cent tomorrow. Do it by the end of the day, she says, and don't tell anyone. What she just did is illegal. Federal employees are barred from using nonpublic information for private gain. Maggie just committed federal insider trading in her own living room.

segments.titre: Day 3: leaked spreadsheet, Tom drains the account, Gene's ATM
segments.resume: A Charlotte bank analyst leaks a spreadsheet ranking regional banks by losses on their IOUs and it goes viral, with Chesapeake Federal near the top. Tom drains his account in eleven minutes, while his neighbor Gene is stuck at an out-of-service ATM.
segments.texte: Day 3 A bank analyst in Charlotte leaks a spreadsheet ranking regional banks by how much they've lost on their IOUs. None of it is secret, exactly, since banks have to report those losses. By lunchtime the spreadsheet has gone viral. Chesapeake Federal is near the top. At 3:52 p.m., Tom rushes into Chesapeake Federal bank. It takes eleven agonizing minutes, two forms, and a manager's signature but he successfully drains the account. As Tom walks to his car, he spots his neighbor, Gene standing at the ATM, punching the buttons. Suddenly a message flashes up, “Temporarily out of service” and his card is spat back out. Gene looks up and sees Tom. He gives a wave. Tom waves back, and hurries to his car. Tom got his money out. Gene isn’t so lucky.

segments.titre: Day 4: the run on Chesapeake Federal begins
segments.resume: By 8 a.m. Friday a line of panicked customers stretches around the block, the manager hands out numbered tickets and a teller reads that deposits are safe and insured. Gene, number forty-three, has payroll for 14 landscaping employees and received the spreadsheet from his nephew at 6 a.m.
segments.texte: Day 4 By 8 a.m. on Friday morning the spreadsheet has done its work. The branch manager at Chesapeake Federal has set up a folding chair by the door. He’s handing out numbered deli counter tickets to a line of panicked customers that stretches around the block. Inside, a teller reads from a laminated sheet: “Your deposits are safe and insured.” Gene Albright is number forty-three. His payroll went out by direct deposit on Wednesday, the way it always does, so the 14 guys at his landscaping company get paid Friday. Gene’s nephew sent him the spreadsheet at 6 a.m. with no context. It’s the classic sign to panic.

segments.titre: Deposit insurance limit: $250,000 and uninsured deposits
segments.resume: Maggie watches the line and knows the truth: the government insures deposits up to $250,000 per person, per bank. Gene's business account holds $412,000 for payroll, taxes and a truck, and at Silicon Valley Bank about 94% of deposits exceeded the insured limit.
segments.texte: 8 miles (13 km) away, Maggie is watching the same line on a muted television in the office kitchen. The words on the teller’s laminated card are close to ones she has written herself a dozen times. But she knows the truth. The government insures bank deposits up to $250,000 per person, per bank. Above that, you’re on your own. Gene's business account holds $412,000, which is payroll, quarterly taxes, and the down payment on a new truck. He isn't unusual. At Silicon Valley Bank, about 94% of all deposits were over the limit, and therefore uninsured.

segments.titre: Branch runs out of cash; regulators seize the bank
segments.resume: The branch runs out of cash at 11:40 and the manager tells everyone to come back Monday. At 6 p.m. regulators lock the doors and take over Chesapeake Federal, freezing Gene's payroll that was still moving through the bank's systems.
segments.texte: The branch runs out of cash at 11:40. The manager stands on the folding chair and tells everyone to come back Monday. At 6 p.m., regulators lock the doors of Chesapeake Federal and take it over. Gene's payroll, which left his account Wednesday and was still moving through the bank's systems, freezes in place.

segments.titre: Day 5: Buenos Aires and Argentina's 2001 bank freeze
segments.resume: Maggie and Tom's daughter Lucía, teaching English in Buenos Aires, finds her landlady Señora Ferrer watching the news. Ferrer lived through Argentina's 2001 collapse, when all bank accounts were frozen, withdrawals limited to 250 pesos a week and the president resigned 19 days later; Argentines keep about $271 billion in foreign cash outside banks.
segments.texte: Day 5 Maggie and Tom’s 24 year old daughter Lucía is in Buenos Aires teaching English. Every month, her parents wire her money. Today, she comes downstairs to find her landlady glued to CNN en Español. Señora Ferrer lived through Argentina’s catastrophic collapse in 2001 when the government froze every bank account in the country. People could only take out 250 pesos a week. Nineteen days later the president resigned. Ever since, many Argentines have kept their savings where no government can reach them, about $271 billion in foreign cash outside the banks, much of it in dollars “stashed away in mattresses” at home. Senora Ferrer points at the screen with her cigarette and warns the first thing governments tell you is that your money is safe. That night, for the first time in history, Argentinians wonder about keeping dollars under their mattresses.

segments.titre: Day 6: rating downgrade and the cost of losing the AAA
segments.resume: Credit rating agencies strip America's financial shield: Moody's removed the last AAA in May 2025 and another agency downgrades further. The top rating held borrowing costs about 1.6 points lower, worth $640 billion a year or nearly $1,900 per person, and Niall Ferguson warned that spending more on interest than defense signals collapse, a line America crossed in 2024.
segments.texte: Day 6 By Sunday, the credit rating agencies are circling like vultures, stripping America of its financial shield. Moody’s already took away America's last AAA rating in May 2025. Now another agency knocks it down a notch further. America has had the world's best credit score for 80 years, and that has kept its borrowing costs about 1.6 percentage points lower than they should be. Spread across $40 trillion of debt, 1.6 points works out to $640 billion a year. That’s nearly $1,900 for every person in the country. Interest on the debt already runs past $1 trillion a year. The historian Niall Ferguson warned that when a superpower starts spending more on interest than it does on national defense, its collapse is imminent. America crossed that line in 2024.

segments.titre: The President's address: bluff about guaranteed deposits
segments.resume: At 9 p.m. the President addresses the nation from the Oval Office, declaring the dollar unshakeable and every bank deposit fully guaranteed. Maggie knows he is bluffing because the government is printing money it does not have to back promises it cannot keep.
segments.texte: At 9 p.m., the President addresses the nation from the Oval Office. He declares that the dollar is unshakeable and that every single bank deposit in America is fully guaranteed. Maggie watches from her couch. She knows the President is bluffing. The government is printing money it doesn’t have, to back promises it can’t keep.

segments.titre: Day 7: Gene's receiver's certificate and workers demand cash
segments.resume: A bank in Rockville that bought the remains of Chesapeake Federal pays Gene his insured $250,000, while the other $162,000 becomes a receiver's certificate, a vague promise of repayment in years. His crew is paid 3 days late and two men quit, demanding physical cash.
segments.texte: Day 7 On Monday, Gene's insured $250,000 shows up at a bank in Rockville that bought what was left of Chesapeake Federal. The other $162,000 becomes a receiver's certificate, a vague promise that in a few years, he might get some of it back… if he’s lucky. Gene now owns an IOU of his own. His crew gets paid Monday afternoon, 3 days late. Two of his men quit on the spot. They demand to be paid in physical cash. And they’re not the only ones.

segments.titre: Day 8: Rosa's frozen money market fund
segments.resume: Maggie's 79 year old mother Rosa in Tucson finds her retirement account frozen: her money market fund held IOUs from regional banks including Chesapeake Federal. Maggie promises the money will return and then realizes she broke the law to protect her husband's cash without warning her own mother.
segments.texte: Day 8 In Tucson, Maggie’s 79 year old mother, Rosa tries to check her retirement savings on her phone. The app won't load. Instead there's a notice: the account is frozen. Rosa’s life savings were parked in a money market fund she was told was as good as cash. For most of her life, that was true. But the fund was stuffed with IOUs from a handful of regional banks. One of them was Chesapeake Federal. The financial contagion has wiped out the elderly. Rosa calls Maggie in a panic. Maggie is standing in a hallway at the Treasury, pressing her phone to her ear. She promises that the money will return. She doesn’t say when. Rosa’s rent comes due on the first, and Maggie says she'll send money. Then a sickening realization hits Maggie. She broke the law to save her husband’s cash a week ago. She didn’t even think to warn her own mother.

segments.titre: Day 12: flight from the dollar with nowhere to go
segments.resume: The world wants out of dollars but the euro is the only real alternative and China's currency is about 2% of reserves, so money runs into gold. China and Hong Kong hold $962 billion of Treasuries and cannot dump them without hurting themselves, like two people handcuffed together; in Buenos Aires Ferrer queues to buy gold.
segments.texte: Day 12 The entire global financial market is sprinting for the exits. The world wants out of dollars, but there isn't anywhere big enough to go. The Euro is the only real alternative. China's currency makes up about 2% of the world's reserves. So the money runs into gold And the biggest sellers can't really sell. China and Hong Kong hold $962 billion of American IOUs. If they dump it, they destroy themselves. America and its creditors are like two people handcuffed together in a burning building, each pulling toward a different door. In Buenos Aires, Lucía sends her parents a photo of a line outside a currency exchange, wrapping around the block. Her elderly landlord is in it, clutching her purse. The text says, “She's buying gold. She says you should too.”

segments.titre: Day 14: the Fed prints money and the dollar's worst day
segments.resume: With no buyers, the Federal Reserve starts creating trillions of dollars to buy back its own bonds, which can save either the bonds and the government or the dollar, but not both. The dollar posts its worst day in decades and Tom notices filling the tank costs $11 more than two weeks ago.
segments.texte: Day 14 With no one on Earth buying dollars, the Federal Reserve plays its last desperate card. It triggers the money printers. They begin typing trillions of phantom dollars into existence, to buy back their own worthless IOUs. Maggie drafts the emergency statement, forcing herself to type: the markets remain orderly. The Fed can print money to save the bonds and the government or it can save the dollar. It can’t do both. By late afternoon, the dollar has posted its worst day in decades. That evening, Tom walks into the kitchen and drops a gas receipt on the counter. Filling the tank cost an extra $11 more than it did 2 weeks ago.

segments.titre: Day 15: import prices and creeping inflation
segments.resume: Tom's frame shipment arrives but his Chinese supplier raises every price 18% and demands upfront payment. A weaker dollar raises import prices, about a third of a drop passing through, with gas rising first, then coffee and bananas, creeping up a few cents at a time.
segments.texte: Day 15 Tom’s container of bike frames arrives in Baltimore. Tom pays for it with the money Maggie told him to move. But the small victory is short lived. The same afternoon, his supplier in China sends next season’s price list. Every frame is 18% more expensive and they’re demanding payment upfront. When the dollar gets weaker, everything America imports gets more expensive. The people selling want the same amount of their own money as before. Economists figure about a third of a drop in the dollar shows up in import prices. Gas goes up first, because oil is priced in dollars and the dollar is buying less of it. Then coffee, then bananas, and everything else. It doesn’t explode overnight, it just creeps up. The prices change on the shelf a few cents at a time. And nobody notices until it’s too late.

segments.titre: Day 21: generic drug shortage and Rosa's pill cutting
segments.resume: Rosa's pharmacy tells her metoprolol, her heart medicine, is on backorder and gives her the last six tablets. About 90% of American prescriptions are generics made from overseas chemical powder, and with the dollar collapsing foreign factories sell to Europe, so Rosa cuts her pills in half.
segments.texte: Day 21 In Tucson, Maggie’s mother walks into her pharmacy to refill her heart medicine. It's metoprolol, one of the most ordinary drugs in America. The pharmacist tells her it's on backorder and gives her the six tablets they have left. About 90% of American prescriptions are generics, and most of them start life as chemical powder from overseas. With the dollar collapsing, foreign factories are selling to Europe instead. Desperate, Rosa gets out a kitchen knife and starts cutting her pills in half.

segments.titre: The social fabric tears: pawn shops, food drives, rumors
segments.resume: Across the country pawn shops hang signs saying they buy euros, a Maryland church moves its food drive from November to now, and a Facebook rumor spreads that the government will seize retirement accounts. People believe it.
segments.texte: Around the country, the social fabric begins to tear. Pawn shops start hanging signs saying “WE BUY EUROS”. A church in Maryland moves its annual food drive from November to now. A rumor spreads on Facebook that the government is about to seize everyone's retirement accounts. And people believe it.

segments.titre: Day 25: Dow record high but purchasing power is dead
segments.resume: The Dow closes at a record high and business anchors cheer, but the Dow is measured in dollars and the dollar is shrinking. Portfolios rise while purchasing power collapses.
segments.texte: Day 25 The Dow closes at a record high. The news anchors on the business channels are ecstatic. What they fail to mention is that the Dow is measured in dollars, and the dollar is shrinking. Portfolios are going up, but purchasing power is dead.

segments.titre: Capital controls: gold ban, frozen wires and FDR's 1933 precedent
segments.resume: Mortgage rates cross 9% and the Treasury imposes emergency capital controls, barring Americans from buying gold or foreign currency and freezing international wires. In 1933 Franklin Roosevelt ordered gold handed over at $20.67 an ounce and revalued it at $35 the next year; Tom's Taiwan payment and Maggie's money for Lucía get stuck.
segments.texte: Mortgage rates cross 9%. House sales are stagnant. To stop money fleeing the country, the Treasury panics and implements emergency capital controls. Americans are barred from buying gold or foreign currency. All international wire transfers are frozen. The country has done this before. In 1933, Franklin Roosevelt ordered Americans to hand over their gold to the government at $20.67 an ounce, and the next year the government revalued gold at $35. Tom's payment to Taiwan gets stuck in review. The money Maggie sends to their daughter in Buenos Aires vanishes. Americans are trapped inside a sinking ship.

segments.titre: Day 31: the Mar-a-Lago Accord and Stephen Miran's idea
segments.resume: Maggie is ordered to draft the term sheet for the Mar-a-Lago Accord, an idea sketched by economist Stephen Miran. Allies would swap their IOUs for 100-year bonds in return for staying under the US military umbrella, with refusers facing heavy tariffs, effectively asking lenders to wait a century and negotiating with aircraft carriers.
segments.texte: Day 31 Maggie is ordered to draft the term sheet for something the White House has started calling the Mar-a-Lago Accord. It’s an idea economist Stephen Miran sketched out before joining the government. America’s allies would swap the IOUs they already own for new ones that don't come due for a 100 years. In return they'd stay under America's military umbrella. The countries that refused would face heavy tariffs. America, in effect, would ask its lenders to wait a century to get paid, and it would negotiate using its aircraft carriers.

segments.titre: Congress subpoena exposes Maggie; she loses her badge
segments.resume: A reporter calls: Congress subpoenaed records of the failed banks and found the exact timestamp of Tom draining his account, with security footage, and his wife works in the Office of Debt Management. By noon Maggie is stripped of her badge and escorted out by the Inspector General, and the story runs as a Treasury official's family pulling cash before the bank run.
segments.texte: Maggie stares at the blank page. Her phone rings before she can write a word. It’s an investigative reporter. Congress has subpoenaed the bank records from the failed banks in their last 48 hours... and one of them is Chesapeake Federal. They have the exact timestamp of a man draining his back account the day before the bank collapsed. A man whose wife works in the Treasury Department's Office of Debt Management. They have the security footage of it happening. The reporter wants to know if Maggie has any comment. By noon Maggie is stripped of her badge and escorted out the building by the Inspector General. The story runs that night under the headline, “Treasury Official's Family Pulled Cash Before Bank Run.” Strangers start slowing down when they drive past the house.

segments.titre: Day 40: Gene confronts Maggie and closes the gate
segments.resume: Gene visits in dirt stained work clothes after reading the article, having seen Tom in the bank parking lot. His company shrank from 14 employees to 4 with debts mounting; he asks if she knew, she says yes, and he leaves, closing the gate the Castellanos had left open for 19 years.
segments.texte: Day 40 Around dinnertime, there’s a heavy knock on Maggie’s front door. It’s Gene. He's in his dirt stained work clothes. He doesn’t come in. Instead he tells her that he read the article. Maggie doesn’t know what to say. Gene tells her he’s not here to make a scene. But he mentions that he saw Tom that day in the parking lot. He says he’s been thinking about that interaction ever since the article came out. He had 14 employees, now he has 4. His company is circling the drain. The collectors are calling. He has mounting debts and no way to pay them. He asks Maggie if she knew. She says yes. Gene nods and thinks it over for a moment. He looks past her, into the warm house and then down at his calloused hands. Without saying a word, he turns and walks down the steps. On his way out he closes the gate at the end of the path, the one the Castellanos have left open for 19 years.

segments.titre: Day 44: creditors' demands and no IMF rescue
segments.resume: Foreign powers say they will keep buying US debt only if America gives up tariffs, export controls and weapons sales, leaving it hostage to its creditors. America cannot get an IMF bailout because it is the largest shareholder, so Congress cuts spending, trimming the Pentagon budget and keeping a carrier group in port.
segments.texte: Day 44 With the dollar shattered, the countries holding America’s IOUs start making demands. Foreign powers inform Washington they’ll only keep buying US debt if America surrenders its tariffs, export controls and weapons sales. America is being held hostage to its creditors. The superpower is broken. The usual way out of a crisis like this is a massive bailout from the IMF. But America can't call the IMF, for the same reason you can't borrow money from your own wallet. The United States is the IMF's largest shareholder. So Congress does the spending cuts on its own. The Pentagon's budget gets trimmed, and a carrier group scheduled to deploy in the spring stays in port.

segments.titre: Rosa runs out of pills and dies on Day 50
segments.resume: Rosa runs out of her half-cut tablets and, with her savings frozen, cannot afford the brand-name version and says she will wait. On Day 50 paramedics find her on the kitchen floor, dead of a heart attack, with an empty pill organizer and a knife coated in white powder beside it.
segments.texte: In Tucson, Rosa runs out of her half-cut tablets. The pharmacy had offered her the brand-name version weeks ago, but her savings are still frozen. She can’t afford it. She tells the pharmacist she’ll wait. Day 50 A neighbor notices that Rosa's newspaper is still in the driveway at noon. The paramedics find her on the kitchen floor. It was her heart and it was over quick. The empty pill organizer lies on the kitchen counter. Next to it is a kitchen knife coated in fine white powder.

segments.titre: Tom closes the bike shop for good
segments.resume: Tom closes the bike shop because the payment to Taiwan never cleared and the spring order never came, while the rent did. He tapes a sign to the door written on the back of the supplier's price list.
segments.texte: Tom closes the bike shop for good. The payment to Taiwan never cleared and the spring order never came. The rent did. He tapes a sign to the door. He writes it on the back of the supplier's price list, because that's the only paper in the shop.

segments.titre: Day 60: Gene's death at his home and the closed gate
segments.resume: Maggie sees flashing blue lights and police tape at Gene's house, neighbors watching, and coroners wheeling a body bag down the driveway. Gene's debts mounted and selling his company did not cover them; Maggie looks at the gate he closed.
segments.texte: Day 60 Maggie stares out the window at the flashing blue lights outside Gene’s house A strip of yellow police tape is stretched across his yard. A small group of neighbors have gathered on the sidewalk, watching in silence. The garage door is halfway open. Maggie can see a heavy beam illuminated by the lights of the squad cars. Two coroners roll a gurney down the driveway, a heavy black body bag strapped to it. Gene’s debts mounted up. He tried to find a buyer for his company, but it wasn’t enough to pay everything off. Maggie looks at the gate at the end of the walk, the one Gene closed a few weeks ago.

segments.titre: Day 70: Lucía returns; the dollar is still the world's trusted bill
segments.resume: Lucía flies home from Buenos Aires, where the money her parents send buys about half as much when it arrives. Her landlady presses a folded American $100 bill into her hand, since the dollar is still the only bill the world trusts, and Tom takes a job assembling bikes in a big-box store at $25 an hour.
segments.texte: Day 70 Lucía flies home from Buenos Aires. The money her parents send now buys about half of what it used to… at least when it arrives at all. Outside the airport, her elderly landlady presses a folded American $100 bill into Lucía's hand and closes her fingers around it. Even now, the American dollar is the only bill the world trusts. Tom takes a job assembling bikes in the back of a big-box store at $25 an hour. He's good at it. His manager is 26 and calls Tom “boss” as a joke. Tom laughs every time, because he needs this job.

segments.titre: Day 90: foreign buyers return to the $42 billion auction
segments.resume: On a Tuesday at 1 p.m. the US again sells $42 billion of 10-year IOUs while Maggie, barred from the Treasury building and under investigation, watches at home. Japan, the Gulf funds and European pension managers are back, proving her theory right while the rules of the game changed.
segments.texte: Day 90 At 1 p.m., on a Tuesday afternoon, the United States sells another $42 billion of 10-year IOUs. Maggie watches from the kitchen table on her own laptop. She isn't allowed in the Treasury building anymore. Her badge is in a drawer somewhere on Pennsylvania Avenue. The investigation into her actions is still open. Nobody has told her when it will close. The results are posted a minute later. The foreign buyers are back. Japan is back. So are the Gulf funds and the European pension managers, the same regulars she used to know by name. Her theory was right the whole time. It’s just the rules of the game changed.

segments.titre: The price of buyers returning: a 6.5% rate for a decade
segments.resume: To bring buyers back America had to offer an astronomical 6.5% interest rate, which commits taxpayers to an extra $500 million a year for 10 years from this single auction. The cost comes out of schools, roads, the Pentagon and eventually paychecks, showing up as a new number on every mortgage, car loan and credit card.
segments.texte: To get the buyers back, America had to promise an astronomical 6.5% interest rate. On this single afternoon, American taxpayers signed over an extra $500 million a year, every year, for the next 10 years. It comes out of the schools, and the roads, and the Pentagon, and eventually out of everyone's paycheck. Nobody will notice. There will just be a new number on every mortgage, every car loan and every credit card statement for the rest of Maggie's life.

segments.titre: The end of the dollar's reign is the loss of its privilege
segments.resume: The dollar remains the dominant currency because nothing can replace it: the euro is still the euro and China's currency is mostly stuck inside China. What is gone is the privilege, since for 80 years the world lent America money at a discount and now lends at the going rate like to anyone else.
segments.texte: That's the strange thing about the end of the dollar's reign. It isn't really the end. The dollar is still the dominant currency in the world, because nothing can get big enough to replace it. The Euro is still the Euro. China's currency is still mostly stuck inside China. What's gone is the privilege. For 80 years, the world lent America money at a discount simply because it was America. Now it lends at the going rate, like it would to anyone else.

segments.titre: Hoover Institution model: 7.6% weaker dollar, 0.9 points higher rates
segments.resume: Economists writing for Stanford's Hoover Institution modeled the dollar losing its special status entirely and found it would settle about 7.6% weaker, with long-term rates about 0.9 percentage points higher. The crisis is technically survivable, but the models describe where you land, not how hard you fall.
segments.texte: Economists writing for Stanford's Hoover Institution modeled this exact scenario. They asked what would happen if the dollar lost its special status entirely, and found that once everything settled, the dollar would end up about 7.6% weaker. Long-term interest rates were about 0.9 percentage points higher. The crisis is technically survivable. But the models only describe where you land. Not where you fall.

segments.titre: Closing: the Treasury statement and the Japanese yen video
segments.resume: At 1:24 the Treasury posts its statement saying the auction was well received, a template Maggie wrote herself years ago. The video ends by pointing to the video The Japanese Yen is Collapsing and Threatening America about another ticking financial time bomb.
segments.texte: At 1:24, the Treasury posts its statement. Maggie doesn't have to open it. She wrote the template herself, years ago. The auction was well received. The U.S. isn’t the only country facing a ticking financial time bomb. Watch “The Japanese Yen is Collapsing and Threatening America” to see how it could hit your pocket. Or click on this.
